slides.say: Now a new question. Two circles with the same center have radii r and one point three r. Noah says that the outer circumference is one point three times the inner circumference. Emma says that the area of the ring between the circles is bigger than the area of the inner circle. Who is right?
So we check two claims, and decide who is right. Noah, Emma, both, or neither. We'll solve it in two different ways.
Let's start with the math way, with the circle formulas and no similarity. Noah talks about circumferences. The circumference of a circle is two pi r.
The outer radius is one point three r. Two times one point three is two point six. So the outer circumference is two point six pi r.
The inner radius is r, so the inner circumference is two pi r.
Two point six is one point three times two. So the outer circumference is one point three times the inner one. Noah is right.
at: Two point six is one point three times

slides.say: So the choices that say Noah is wrong are out. Neither is choice number three, and Emma only is choice number four.

slides: Now it's Noah only, or both of them.

slides.say: Now Emma. She says the ring is bigger than the inner circle. The ring is the big circle minus the small circle.
at: The ring is the big circle

slides.say: The big circle is pi, times the square of one point three r. One point three squared is one point six nine, because thirteen squared is a hundred sixty-nine.
So the big circle is one point six nine pi r squared.
The small circle is pi r squared. So the ring is one point six nine minus one, zero point six nine pi r squared.
at: So the ring is one point six nine minus

slides.say: The inner circle is one pi r squared. Zero point six nine is less than one. So the ring is smaller, and Emma is wrong.
at: Zero point six nine is less

slides: In the figure, the ring may look big. Our eye isn't good at comparing a ring with a circle, so we calculate.

slides.say: So only Noah is right. That's choice number two. Now a shorter way, with similarity.
Now by understanding, with similarity. Similar shapes aren't only triangles. Any two circles are similar, like any two squares or two regular hexagons.

slides: First, Noah's claim. In similar shapes, every line keeps the linear ratio. The radius is one point three times as big. So the circumference is one point three times as big too. No calculation. Noah is right.
Now Emma's claim. From the linear ratio to the area ratio, we square. But one to one point three isn't comfortable. We don't like decimals.

slides.say: So let's expand the ratio to whole numbers. We multiply both numbers by ten. One to one point three is the same ratio as ten to thirteen.
at: One to one point three is the same

slides.say: We didn't change the ratio. We only made it easier to work with. Now we square both numbers. Ten squared is a hundred, and thirteen squared is a hundred sixty-nine.
So the inner circle is a hundred ratio units, and the big circle is a hundred sixty-nine units.
at: So the inner circle is a hundred

slides.say: The ring is a hundred sixty-nine minus a hundred, sixty-nine units. Sixty-nine is less than a hundred. So the ring is smaller, and Emma is wrong.
at: The ring is a hundred sixty-nine

slides.say: Questions like this one are much shorter with similarity. Choice number two is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number two is our answer
